```{julia}
#| output: false

# The example system: two cities, three facilities (1 = WTE, 2 = MRF, 3 = LF)
waste = [100, 170]                              # [Mg/day] produced by each city
capacity = [150, 130, 200]                      # [Mg/day] each facility can take
fixed_cost_year = [900_000, 400_000, 700_000]   # [$/yr] if the facility operates
fixed_cost = round.(Int, fixed_cost_year ./ 365)   # [$/day]
tipping = [60, 5, 40]                           # [$/Mg] handled at each facility
recycle_rate = 0.4                              # fraction of MRF input recycled
recycle_cost = 35                               # [$/Mg recycled]
ash_rate = 0.2                                  # fraction of WTE input left as ash
transport_rate = 1.5                            # [$/Mg-km]
city_distance = [15 5 30; 10 15 25]             # [km] from city i to facility j
mrf_to_wte, mrf_to_lf, wte_to_lf = 15, 32, 18   # [km] residual routes

# Cost of sending 1 Mg from city i to facility j: haul it, tip it, and
# (at the MRF) pay to recycle the fraction that is recovered
city_cost = zeros(2, 3)
for i in 1:2
    for j in 1:3
        city_cost[i, j] = transport_rate * city_distance[i, j] + tipping[j]
        if j == 2
            city_cost[i, j] = city_cost[i, j] + recycle_rate * recycle_cost
        end
    end
end
cost_R21 = transport_rate * mrf_to_wte + tipping[1]   # MRF residual to WTE
cost_R23 = transport_rate * mrf_to_lf + tipping[3]    # MRF residual to LF
cost_R13 = transport_rate * wte_to_lf + tipping[3]    # WTE ash to LF

# Print whole numbers without a decimal point
function fmt(x)
    rounded_x = round(x; digits=1)
    if isinteger(rounded_x)
        return string(Int(rounded_x))
    end
    return string(rounded_x)
end
commas(n) = replace(string(round(Int, n)), r"(?<=\d)(?=(\d{3})+$)" => ",")
```

# Review of Last Class

## Indicator Variables and Mixed Integer Programming

Binary decisions need **indicator variables** $u \in \{0, 1\}$:

- changes decision problem to **mixed integer**;
- write **conditional** constraints or objectives using indicators;
- basic solution algorithm is **branch and bound**.

# Solid Waste Management

## Waste Load Allocation

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width=50%}
Some relevant questions:

- Where do we send waste?
- What types of facilities do we build/operate?
:::
::: {.column width=50%}

![Waste Management Hierarchy](https://www.epa.gov/sites/default/files/styles/medium/public/2015-08/hierarchy_hierarchy_and_options_pages.png){width=100%}

::: {.caption}
Source: [EPA](https://www.epa.gov/homeland-security-waste/waste-management-options-homeland-security-incidents)
:::
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
Waste management options form a hierarchy: reduce first, then recycle, then recover energy, and landfill last. There are a variety of types of facilities, and a waste management plan requires deciding which facilities to build or operate.
:::

## Waste Allocation As A Network

Waste moves as *flows* between waste sources and sinks (disposal sites) based on transportation networks.

![Network Representation](figures/waste-network-blank.svg){width=75%}

::: {.notes}
A network has nodes and edges. We want to decide how to allocate waste given the restrictions of the road network as well as processing any residual waste.
:::

## Network and Decision Parameterization

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width=50%}
![Network Parameterization](figures/waste-network-params.svg)
:::
::: {.column width=50%}

| Variable | Definition |
| :--: | :------- |
| $\color{purple}S_i$ | Waste produced at source $i$ (Mg/day) |
| $\color{red}K_j$ | Capacity of disposal $j$ (Mg/day) |
| $\color{blue}W_{ij}$ | Waste transported from source $i$ to disposal $j$ (Mg/day) |

:::
::::
## Conservation at Each Node

**Mass balance** holds at each facility:

- A waste source does not hold onto any waste, $\sum_j W_{ij} = S_i$,
- Incoming flows at a disposal facility have to balance with waste disposal and outflows of residual waste (*e.g.* material that cannot be recycled).

# Waste Management Example

## Example System

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width=60%}
![Waste Management Example](figures/waste-example-network.svg)
:::
::: {.column width=40%}
Three disposal options:

- Waste-to-Energy (WTE)
- Materials Recovery Facility (MRF)
- Landfill (LF)

We do not have to operate all of the facilities if they are not needed.
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
Two cities, producing 100 and 170 Mg/day, and three facilities with the capacities in red. Distances in blue. Note the edges between facilities: the MRF sends its residual to the WTE or the landfill, and the WTE sends its ash to the landfill.
:::

## Decision Variables

***What are our decision variables?***

::: {.fragment .fade-in}
Variable | Definition
:--: | :-----
$W_{ij}$ | Waste transported from city $i$ to disposal $j$ (Mg/day)
$R_{kj}$ | Residual waste transported from disposal $k$ to disposal $j$ (Mg/day)
$Y_j$ | Operational status (on/off) of disposal $j$ (binary)
:::

## Objective: Minimize Costs

- **Transportation**: transporting waste has a per-weight cost $a_{ij}$ (\$/Mg-km) times the distance $l_{ij}$ (km).
- **Disposal**: facilities have a fixed cost to operate $c_j$ (\$/day) and a variable tipping cost $b_j$ (\$/Mg).

::: {.fragment .fade-in}
$$Y_j = \begin{cases}0 & \text{if facility } j \text{ is not operated} \\ 1 & \text{if facility } j \text{ is operated} \end{cases}$$

$$\text{Disposal cost} = \sum_j \left[c_j \, Y_j + b_j \times (\text{everything arriving at } j)\right]$$
:::

## Costs For Our Example

```{julia}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis

println("| Facility | Fixed cost (\\\$/yr) | Fixed cost (\\\$/day) | Tipping (\\\$/Mg) | Capacity (Mg/day) |")
println("|:--|--:|--:|--:|--:|")
for j in 1:3
    println("| ", ["WTE", "MRF", "LF"][j], " | ", commas(fixed_cost_year[j]), " | ", commas(fixed_cost[j]),
        " | ", tipping[j], " | ", capacity[j], " |")
end
```

Transport costs \$`{julia} @sprintf("%.2f", transport_rate)`/Mg-km. The MRF recycles `{julia} round(Int, 100 * recycle_rate)`% of what it receives, at \$`{julia} recycle_cost`/Mg recycled, and passes on the rest; the WTE leaves `{julia} round(Int, 100 * ash_rate)`% of its input as ash.

::: {.notes}
The daily fixed costs are the annual costs divided by 365. The MRF is cheap to run but does not dispose of the rest: the `{julia} round(Int, 100 * (1 - recycle_rate))`% it does not recycle still has to go to the WTE or the landfill.
:::


## Mass Balance for Sources and Residuals

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width=45%}
**Cities** ship everything they produce:

$W_{11} + W_{12} + W_{13} =$ `{julia} waste[1]`

$W_{21} + W_{22} + W_{23} =$ `{julia} waste[2]`
:::
::: {.column width=55%}
::: {.fragment .fade-in}
**Residuals** (partial outflows after processing):

WTE ash:
$$R_{13} = 0.2\,(W_{11} + W_{21} + R_{21})$$

MRF residual:
$$R_{21} + R_{23} = 0.6\,(W_{12} + W_{22})$$
:::
:::
::::

## Capacity Constraints

Need to modify capacity constraints to ensure that a closed facility receives no waste:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{WTE:}& \quad W_{11} + W_{21} + R_{21} \leq 150\,Y_1 \\
\text{MRF:}& \quad W_{12} + W_{22} \leq 130\,Y_2 \\
\text{LF:}& \quad W_{13} + W_{23} + R_{13} + R_{23} \leq 200\,Y_3
\end{aligned}
$$


## The Full Problem

$$
\begin{aligned}
\min_{\mathbf{W}, \mathbf{R}, \mathbf{Y}} \quad & \sum_{i, j} C_{ij} W_{ij} + \sum_{k, j} C^R_{kj} R_{kj} + \sum_j c_j Y_j \\
\text{subject to:} \quad & \textstyle\sum_j W_{ij} = S_i \\
& \text{residual out of } k = \text{fraction} \times \text{input to } k \\
& \textstyle\sum_i W_{ij} + \sum_k R_{kj} \leq K_j\,Y_j \\
& W_{ij},\, R_{kj} \geq 0, \quad Y_j \in \{0, 1\}
\end{aligned}
$$

$C_{ij}$, $C^R_{kj}$: cost per Mg sent from city $i$, or of residual sent from facility $k$, to facility $j$ (\$/Mg): haul, tip and, at the MRF, recycle.

::: {.notes}
The same problem in general form. It is a mixed integer linear program: linear in everything, with three binary variables.
:::

# Solving It

## Solving the Example in JuMP

```{julia}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: true
#| output: false

function solve_waste(; landfill_capacity=capacity[3])
    cap = [capacity[1], capacity[2], landfill_capacity]
    model = Model(HiGHS.Optimizer)
    set_silent(model)
    @variable(model, W[1:2, 1:3] >= 0)        # city i -> facility j [Mg/day]
    @variable(model, R21 >= 0)                # MRF residual -> WTE
    @variable(model, R23 >= 0)                # MRF residual -> LF
    @variable(model, R13 >= 0)                # WTE ash -> LF
    @variable(model, Y[1:3], Bin)             # facility operates?
    @objective(model, Min, sum(city_cost[i, j] * W[i, j] for i in 1:2, j in 1:3) +
        cost_R21 * R21 + cost_R23 * R23 + cost_R13 * R13 + sum(fixed_cost[j] * Y[j] for j in 1:3))
    @constraint(model, city[i in 1:2], sum(W[i, :]) == waste[i])
    @constraint(model, ash, R13 == ash_rate * (W[1, 1] + W[2, 1] + R21))
    @constraint(model, residual, R21 + R23 == (1 - recycle_rate) * (W[1, 2] + W[2, 2]))
    @constraint(model, wte, W[1, 1] + W[2, 1] + R21 <= cap[1] * Y[1])
    @constraint(model, mrf, W[1, 2] + W[2, 2] <= cap[2] * Y[2])
    @constraint(model, lf, W[1, 3] + W[2, 3] + R13 + R23 <= cap[3] * Y[3])
    optimize!(model)
    return (cost=objective_value(model), W=value.(W), R21=value(R21), R23=value(R23),
        R13=value(R13), Y=round.(Int, value.(Y)),
        lf_load=value(W[1, 3] + W[2, 3] + R13 + R23), cap=cap)
end

base = solve_waste()
```

The optimal cost is **\$`{julia} commas(base.cost)`/day**, and all `{julia} sum(base.Y)` facilities operate.

::: {.notes}
Open the fold: each constraint from the previous slides appears once, with Y declared `Bin` and each capacity multiplied by Y.
:::

## The Solution

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width=55%}
![Waste Management Problem Solution](figures/waste-example-solution.svg)
:::
::: {.column width=45%}
| Flow | Mg/day |
|:--|--:|
| City 1 → MRF | `{julia} fmt(base.W[1, 2])` |
| City 2 → LF | `{julia} fmt(base.W[2, 3])` |
| MRF residual → WTE | `{julia} fmt(base.R21)` |
| MRF residual → LF | `{julia} fmt(base.R23)` |
| WTE ash → LF | `{julia} fmt(base.R13)` |
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
City 1 sends everything to the nearby MRF. City 2 sends everything to the landfill. The MRF's residual is split between the WTE and the landfill, and the WTE's ash goes to the landfill too.
:::

## Why Is the WTE Open?

The WTE costs \$`{julia} commas(fixed_cost[1])`/day just to open. **Why pay that to burn `{julia} fmt(base.R21)` Mg/day?**

::: {.fragment .fade-in}
Because the **landfill is full**: it takes `{julia} fmt(base.lf_load)` of its `{julia} capacity[3]` Mg/day. The MRF's residual has to go somewhere, and the only other place is the WTE.

The landfill's capacity constraint is **binding**.
:::

::: {.notes}
Likely question: why is the WTE open if it is expensive? Because the landfill is exactly full, and the MRF's residual has to go somewhere.
:::

## What If the Landfill Were Bigger?

```{julia}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: true
#| output: asis

bigger = solve_waste(landfill_capacity=220)
println("| Landfill capacity (Mg/day) | Cost (\\\$/day) | WTE | MRF | LF |")
println("|:--|--:|:--:|:--:|:--:|")
for r in (base, bigger)
    status = fill("open", 3)
    for j in 1:3
        if r.Y[j] == 0
            status[j] = "**closed**"
        end
    end
    println("| ", r.cap[3], " | ", commas(r.cost), " | ", join(status, " | "), " |")
end
```

With `{julia} bigger.cap[3] - base.cap[3]` Mg/day more landfill, the **WTE closes** and the system saves \$`{julia} commas(base.cost - bigger.cost)`/day. City 2 now sends `{julia} fmt(bigger.W[2, 2])` Mg/day to the MRF, and all `{julia} fmt(bigger.R23)` Mg/day of the MRF's residual goes to the landfill.

::: {.notes}
With a `{julia} bigger.cap[3]` Mg/day landfill, the MRF's residual fits in the landfill and the WTE is no longer worth its fixed cost.
:::

# Key Takeaways

## Key Takeaways

- A network model's decisions are **flows** on arcs, constrained by **conservation** at each node.
- An optional facility needs a **binary**: fixed cost $\times\, Y_j$ in the objective, and in every constraint that changes when it is closed (here, flow in $\leq K_j Y_j$).
- A binding capacity at one facility can force another to open: the WTE runs only because the landfill is full.
- A network graph becomes a model only with fate and transport, costs, and rules.

## Network Models Elsewhere

- Can have more advanced network models with highly-specified routes
  - Transportation networks
  - Power transmission networks
  - Pipeline networks
- Can also add flow constraints rather than just mass-balance.
- Flows could also be bidirectional.

::: {.notes}
The same structure (flows on arcs, conservation at nodes, capacities, sometimes on/off decisions) covers transportation, power transmission, and pipelines. Power flow adds physics that determines how flow splits across lines, rather than letting the planner choose freely.
:::

# Appendix

## Indicator Constraints in JuMP

```julia
@variable(waste, Y[1:3], Bin)
@constraint(waste, commit_mrf, !Y[2] => {W[1, 2] + W[2, 2] == 0})
```

Some solvers let you write the on/off logic directly. This says: if $Y_2 = 0$, nothing arrives at the MRF, $W_{12} + W_{22} = 0$. For the WTE, the arriving flow also includes the MRF residual: $W_{11} + W_{21} + R_{21} = 0$ when $Y_1 = 0$.

The capacity-linking constraint used in the lecture does the same job and works with every solver.

::: {.notes}
Reference only. Indicator constraints are a convenience some solvers support. The linking constraint, arriving flow at most capacity times Y, is the portable way to write the same logic.
:::

## Big-M Reformulation

Not every solver supports indicator constraints. The general trick is a **big-M** constraint:

$$M\,Y_2 \geq W_{12} + W_{22}, \qquad M\,Y_1 \geq W_{11} + W_{21} + R_{21}$$

where $M$ is larger than any feasible value of the right-hand side.

Choosing $M = K_j$ (the facility's capacity) gives exactly the capacity-linking constraint from the lecture.

::: {.notes}
Reference only. A smaller valid M gives a tighter LP relaxation, which helps branch and bound; the capacity is the natural choice here because no feasible flow can exceed it.
:::
